subsection: 2. Role, status, socio-economic groupings, social mobility

notes.b: A status is a position a person holds within a group or society. Each person holds several statuses at the same time.
points: A status is a social position, such as mother, teacher, employee or citizen.
An ascribed status is given at birth or without choice, for example sex, ethnic origin or the family into which a person is born.
An achieved status is gained through effort or choice, for example a qualification, a job or a marriage.
A master status is a status that dominates how others see a person and outweighs the person's other statuses, for example being a serving prisoner.
Societies that allocate status mainly by birth are described as closed; societies that allocate it mainly by achievement are described as open.

notes.b: A role is the behaviour that goes with a status. Roles are learned through socialisation.
points: A role is the set of behaviours and expectations attached to a status.
For example, the role of a student includes attending class, completing homework and respecting the teacher.
Roles change over the life course: a person moves from the role of child to adolescent to adult, and each stage brings different expectations.
Role conflict occurs when the demands of two roles are incompatible, for example a parent who is also a manager and is asked to work late when a child is ill.
Role overload occurs when a person has too many roles and cannot meet all the demands placed on them, for example a working parent who also cares for an elderly relative.
Role conflict and role overload are most common where people hold several demanding roles at once.

notes.b: Socio-economic groups classify people by their economic and social position. They are a form of social stratification.
points: A socio-economic group is a category of people grouped by occupation, income, education, wealth and housing.
Social stratification is the division of a society into layers of unequal rank, and socio-economic groups are its most common measure.
Occupational classifications commonly include professional, managerial and technical, non-manual, skilled manual, semi-skilled and unskilled groups.
Example of a skilled manual occupation: electrician, plumber, carpenter or motor mechanic.
Level of education is one of the strongest factors separating socio-economic groups, because it governs access to skilled and professional work.
Life chances, including educational attainment and health, tend to differ between socio-economic groups.

notes.b: Social mobility is the movement of an individual or a group between socio-economic groups.
points: Upward mobility is movement to a higher socio-economic group, for example a skilled worker who becomes a manager after completing a degree.
Downward mobility is movement to a lower socio-economic group, for example after the loss of a skilled job with no replacement at the same level.
Intergenerational mobility compares a person's position with the position of their parents.
Intragenerational mobility, sometimes called career mobility, compares a person's position at different points in their own working life.
Structural mobility is movement caused by changes in the occupational structure, such as the growth of professional jobs, even when people's relative positions do not change.
Exchange mobility is movement in both directions that balances out, so that the overall pattern of relative positions stays the same.
Factors that help people move up include education and qualifications, skills and training, and access to occupations with promotion prospects.
Barriers to mobility include low family income, lack of access to third-level education, discrimination and living in an area with few employment opportunities.
Social mobility is more likely in an open society, where status is achieved, than in a closed society, where status is ascribed.

keyTerms.definition: A social position a person holds within a group or society.
A status given at birth or without choice, such as sex or family background.
A status gained through effort or choice, such as a qualification or a job.
A status that dominates how others see a person and outweighs their other statuses.
The set of behaviours and expectations attached to a status.
A situation in which the incompatible demands of two roles cannot both be met.
A situation in which a person has too many roles and cannot meet all the demands placed on them.
A category of people grouped by occupation, income, education, wealth and housing.
The division of a society into layers of unequal rank.
The movement of an individual or group between socio-economic groups.
Movement between groups caused by changes in the occupational structure of the economy.
A comparison of a person's socio-economic position with the position of their parents.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between ascribed status and achieved status, giving one example of each.
questions.model: Ascribed status is given at birth or without choice, for example sex, ethnic origin or family background. Achieved status is gained through effort or choice, for example a qualification, a job or a marriage.

questions.prompt: Discuss how role conflict and role overload can arise in family and working life, and explain how education can allow a person to move between socio-economic groups.
questions.model: Role conflict arises when the incompatible demands of two roles cannot both be met, for example a parent who is also a manager and is asked to work late when a child is ill. Role overload arises when a person holds too many roles, for example a working parent who also cares for an elderly relative. Socio-economic groups are categories based on occupation, income, education, wealth and housing. Social mobility is the movement of individuals between these groups. Education is a key route to upward mobility because qualifications open access to skilled and professional occupations. Upward mobility is movement to a higher group, for example a skilled worker who becomes a manager after a degree. Structural mobility also results from changes in the occupational structure. Barriers such as low family income and limited access to third-level education can prevent education from producing mobility.
